newsitem.title: USA: US central bank seen holding interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: US central bank seen holding interest rates steady.

text.p: The Federal Reserve is widely expected to decide to hold interest rates steady at a two-day meeting that begins Tuesday, but many analysts think it is only a matter of time before the U.S. central bank tightens credit.
With inflation tame and and, by at least by one measure, at a 30-year low, the Fed has scant justification for raising short-term rates now, economists said.
"They won't do anything," said Cynthia Latta, of Massachussetts-based economic consultants DRI/McGraw Hill. "There are no signs out there of overheating."

But she and many other analysts expect the central bank to raise rates eventually to counter an anticipated buildup in inflation pressures stemming from a tight labour market and stepped-up wage demands by workers.

Bond prices rose Monday on hopes the Fed will hold rates steady this week. The pace-setting 30-year Treasury issue rose 19/32 of a point, lowering the yield to 6.74 percent from 6.79 percent. Blue-chip stock prices fell slightly.

The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee is slated to begin its two-day meeting at 2:30 p.m. (1930 GMT) on Tuesday. It is not expected to announce its rate decision until around 2:15 p.m. (1915 GMT) on Wednesday.
The Fed has held rates steady for over a year, since cutting them by a quarter of a percentage point on Jan. 31, 1996.
The federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for loans now stands at 5.25 percent. The discount rate the Fed charges on its loans to the banks is 5 percent.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told state governors Sunday that he saw no evidence of significant price pressures in the economy, Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad said.
"He gave a positive report. We've had growth with low inflation," Branstad told reporters after the governors' closed-door meeting with the Fed chief.

Two pet economic indicators of Greenspan's -- the employment cost index, which measures workers' wages and benefits, and the National Association of Purchasing Managers survey -- have shown little sign of inflation pressures.
In public testimony to Congress last month, Greenspan painted a picture of an economy that was surprisingly free of imbalances and inflationary pressures six years into expansion.
But he also warned of the risk that inflation could pick up as workers take advantage of the tight jobs market to demand much higher wages and benefits from their employers.
He also made clear that the Fed would not wait to act until inflation picks up, but would raise rates if it had persuasive evidence that inflation pressures were building.
That is why many analysts believe that a rate increase is likely, perhaps as soon as the Fed's next policy-making meeting March 25.
